overview: Vasicek (1977) was the first model to say the obvious thing about interest rates that Brownian motion refuses to: rates do not wander off to infinity, they get pulled home. The short rate mean-reverts toward a long-run level b at speed a, and that single economic idea buys an affine closed form for the zero coupon bond, P(T) = A(T)e^(−B(T)r₀). Its price here deliberately differs from the market-curve DCF price: Vasicek is a three-parameter *opinion* about discounting, while the curve is a direct quotation — and reading that gap is the lesson.
formula_latex: dr = a(b - r)\,dt + \sigma\,dW, \qquad P(T) = A(T)\,e^{-B(T) r_0}, \quad B(T) = \frac{1 - e^{-aT}}{a}

variables.name: Mean-reversion speed
variables.why_it_matters: How hard rates are pulled home. It caps long-bond risk: B(T) saturates at 1/a, so a 30y bond under Vasicek carries far less rate risk than under a random-walk rate — mean reversion is a promise about the far future.

variables.name: Long-run mean level
variables.why_it_matters: Where rates are headed on average. Calibrated here from the 10y curve point, it anchors long-maturity model yields.

variables.name: Rate volatility
variables.why_it_matters: Absolute (normal) volatility of the short rate. Its convexity gift shows in ln A: volatility *raises* bond prices slightly, because bond prices are convex in rates.

variables.name: Duration factor
variables.why_it_matters: The bond's sensitivity to today's short rate — the model's own modified duration. Watching B bend away from T as maturity grows is watching mean reversion work.

assumptions: One factor: the entire curve is driven by a single short rate — all yields move in near-parallel lockstep.
Normal (Gaussian) rate increments: rates can go negative, which was ridiculed for decades and then happened in Europe and Japan.
Constant a, b, σ through time.
The market price of rate risk is absorbed into the risk-neutral drift.
limitations: Cannot fit today's curve exactly — with three parameters it approximates the curve rather than reproducing it. Hull–White fixes this by making b time-dependent.
One factor cannot produce curve twists or butterflies; steepener trades are invisible to it.
Gaussian tails understate the probability of large rate moves.
Constant volatility across maturities contradicts observed rate-vol term structures.
when_to_use: Teaching mean reversion and affine bond pricing; quick parametric scenario analysis; as the ancestor and sanity check for Hull–White, CIR, and the whole affine family.
when_not_to_use: Anything requiring exact fit to today's curve (use Hull–White), guaranteed positive rates (historically CIR's pitch), or multi-factor curve dynamics (swaptions on curve spreads).
industry_usage: Rarely used raw today, but its skeleton — affine A and B factors — is inside nearly every production rate model; it is the alphabet of the affine language.
comparison_note: Vasicek's gap versus the DCF price is structural, not numerical: DCF reads the discount factor straight off the market curve, while Vasicek generates one from three parameters and a short rate. The difference measures how much of the curve's shape a one-factor mean-reverting model can and cannot capture.
